title: Browser APIs and Persistent Data
keywords: APIs, Asynchronous Operations, and Data Handling
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Browser APIs and Persistent Data in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Browser APIs and Persistent Data within APIs, Asynchronous Operations, and Data Handling. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Remote data can fail, arrive late, or become stale, so data fetching needs explicit cancellation, retry, and empty-state behavior.

content_blocks.title: Browser APIs and Persistent Data: Asynchronous data workflow
content_blocks.alt_text: Asynchronous data workflow diagram for lesson 86: Browser APIs and Persistent Data. Start the request for the current input → Show pending, success, empty, or failure → Cancel stale work and display useful feedback
content_blocks.caption: Data workflow: model all request states and prevent late or failed responses from silently breaking the interface.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: API integration coordinates asynchronous JavaScript, HTTP requests, server data, loading/error states, and configuration across environments. This lesson focuses on Browser APIs and Persistent Data. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: URL state and query parameters
items.text: For URL state and query parameters, keep the URL as the addressable navigation state, use named route records when practical, and handle invalid parameters or failed navigation explicitly. A route guard improves navigation flow but does not replace backend access control.

items.title: Network and online status
items.text: For Network and online status, model pending, success, empty, and failure states. Check HTTP status before treating a response as success, cancel stale work where appropriate, and do not let a late response overwrite newer user intent.

content_blocks.code:
const key = 'vue-demo-theme'
localStorage.setItem(key, 'dark')
const theme = localStorage.getItem(key) ?? 'light'
console.log(theme)
content_blocks.expected_output: The log shows dark after the key is set. Storage may be unavailable or stale and must not hold secrets or authoritative permissions.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the browser Console. Reset with localStorage.removeItem('vue-demo-theme').
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.text: Work through Browser APIs and Persistent Data with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Session storage”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Local storage”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
